Real Analysis — 03 · Differentiation, the Mean Value Theorem and Taylor's Theorem

Created2026-03-27|Updated2026-03-27|Mathematics > Real Analysis
|Post View:

Calculus courses teach the derivative as a set of rules. Analysis asks what the rules rest on. This post defines the derivative as a limit, proves that differentiable functions are continuous, and proves the product and chain rules without the usual gap. The centre of the post is the Mean Value Theorem. It is the one tool that turns information about f′f'f′ into information about fff, and almost every later result depends on it: "zero derivative means constant", L'Hôpital's rule, and Taylor's theorem with a remainder you can actually bound. Along the way you meet functions that break naive intuition: a derivative that exists everywhere but is not continuous, a smooth function whose Taylor series is useless, and a continuous function with no derivative anywhere. It builds on the ε\varepsilonε–δ\deltaδ limits, the Extreme Value Theorem and the Intermediate Value Theorem from post 02.

Series map: 00 The Real Numbers & Completeness → 01 Sequences & Series → 02 Topology of ℝ & Continuity → 03 Differentiation & Taylor's Theorem (this post) → 04 The Riemann Integral → 05 Uniform Convergence & Power Series.

Learning Outcome

  • Define the derivative as a limit of difference quotients and compute it from the definition.
  • Prove that a function differentiable at a point is continuous there, and show with ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣ that the converse fails.
  • Prove the product rule and the chain rule, using the "linear approximation" form of the derivative to avoid dividing by zero.
  • State and prove the Interior Extremum Theorem, Rolle's Theorem, the Mean Value Theorem and Cauchy's Generalised Mean Value Theorem.
  • Use the Mean Value Theorem to prove "f′=0f' = 0f′=0 implies constant", monotonicity tests and numeric inequalities.
  • State and prove Darboux's theorem, and explain why x2sin⁡(1/x)x^2\sin(1/x)x2sin(1/x) matters.
  • Apply L'Hôpital's rule with all of its hypotheses checked.
  • State and prove Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder, and use it to get a proven error bound.
  • Place the smooth non-analytic function e−1/x2e^{-1/x^2}e−1/x2 and Weierstrass's nowhere-differentiable function in the hierarchy of smoothness.

Chapter 1 — The derivative as a limit

Terminology

  • Interval — in this post, III always means an interval of R\mathbb{R}R with more than one point.
  • Difference quotient — for x≠cx \neq cx=c, the slope of the secant line through (c,f(c))(c, f(c))(c,f(c)) and (x,f(x))(x, f(x))(x,f(x)), that is f(x)−f(c)x−c\frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}x−cf(x)−f(c)​.
  • Derivative at a point — the limit of the difference quotient as x→cx \to cx→c, when that limit exists as a real number.
  • One-sided derivative — the same limit taken only from the right (x→c+x \to c^+x→c+) or only from the left. At an endpoint of a closed interval only one side makes sense, and "differentiable at the endpoint" means the one-sided derivative exists.
  • Differentiable on an interval — differentiable at every point of it.
  • Class CkC^kCk — Ck(I)C^k(I)Ck(I) is the set of functions whose first kkk derivatives exist on III and whose kkk-th derivative is continuous. C∞C^\inftyC∞ means derivatives of every order exist.

Definition

Let f:I→Rf : I \to \mathbb{R}f:I→R and c∈Ic \in Ic∈I. Then fff is differentiable at ccc if the limit

f′(c)=lim⁡x→cf(x)−f(c)x−cf'(c) = \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} f′(c)=x→clim​x−cf(x)−f(c)​

exists (as a real number). In ε\varepsilonε–δ\deltaδ form: for every ε>0\varepsilon > 0ε>0 there is δ>0\delta > 0δ>0 such that 0<∣x−c∣<δ0 < \lvert x - c\rvert < \delta0<∣x−c∣<δ and x∈Ix \in Ix∈I imply

∣f(x)−f(c)x−c−f′(c)∣<ε.\left\lvert \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} - f'(c) \right\rvert < \varepsilon. ​x−cf(x)−f(c)​−f′(c)​<ε.

Writing x=c+hx = c + hx=c+h gives the equivalent form f′(c)=lim⁡h→0f(c+h)−f(c)hf'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c+h) - f(c)}{h}f′(c)=limh→0​hf(c+h)−f(c)​.

Worked example. For f(x)=x2f(x) = x^2f(x)=x2 and c=3c = 3c=3:

x2−9x−3=x+3(x≠3),sof′(3)=lim⁡x→3(x+3)=6.\frac{x^2 - 9}{x - 3} = x + 3 \quad (x \neq 3), \qquad \text{so} \qquad f'(3) = \lim_{x \to 3} (x + 3) = 6. x−3x2−9​=x+3(x=3),sof′(3)=x→3lim​(x+3)=6.

The cancellation is legal because the limit never looks at x=3x = 3x=3 itself.

Worked example: the absolute value at 0. For f(x)=∣x∣f(x) = \lvert x\rvertf(x)=∣x∣ the difference quotient at 000 is ∣x∣x\frac{\lvert x\rvert}{x}x∣x∣​, which is 111 for x>0x > 0x>0 and −1-1−1 for x<0x < 0x<0. The right-hand limit is 111, the left-hand limit is −1-1−1, so the two-sided limit does not exist. The function ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣ is continuous at 0 but not differentiable there. Its graph has a corner.

Differentiable implies continuous

Theorem. If f:I→Rf : I \to \mathbb{R}f:I→R is differentiable at ccc, then fff is continuous at ccc.

Proof. For x≠cx \neq cx=c,

f(x)−f(c)=f(x)−f(c)x−c⋅(x−c).f(x) - f(c) = \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} \cdot (x - c). f(x)−f(c)=x−cf(x)−f(c)​⋅(x−c).

As x→cx \to cx→c the first factor tends to f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) and the second tends to 000. By the product rule for limits (post 01, carried over to functions via sequences in post 02), f(x)−f(c)→f′(c)⋅0=0f(x) - f(c) \to f'(c) \cdot 0 = 0f(x)−f(c)→f′(c)⋅0=0. So lim⁡x→cf(x)=f(c)\lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c)limx→c​f(x)=f(c). ■\blacksquare■

The converse is false: ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣ is continuous at 0 and not differentiable there. Chapter 7 shows something much stronger: a function can be continuous everywhere and differentiable nowhere.

The linear-approximation form (Carathéodory)

The following reformulation removes every risky division from later proofs.

Lemma. fff is differentiable at ccc if and only if there is a function φ:I→R\varphi : I \to \mathbb{R}φ:I→R that is continuous at ccc and satisfies

f(x)−f(c)=φ(x) (x−c)for all x∈I.f(x) - f(c) = \varphi(x)\,(x - c) \quad \text{for all } x \in I. f(x)−f(c)=φ(x)(x−c)for all x∈I.

In that case f′(c)=φ(c)f'(c) = \varphi(c)f′(c)=φ(c).

Proof. If f′(c)f'(c)f′(c) exists, define φ(x)=f(x)−f(c)x−c\varphi(x) = \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}φ(x)=x−cf(x)−f(c)​ for x≠cx \neq cx=c and φ(c)=f′(c)\varphi(c) = f'(c)φ(c)=f′(c). The identity holds (at x=cx = cx=c both sides are 0) and φ\varphiφ is continuous at ccc by the definition of f′(c)f'(c)f′(c). Conversely, if such a φ\varphiφ exists, then for x≠cx \neq cx=c the difference quotient equals φ(x)\varphi(x)φ(x), which tends to φ(c)\varphi(c)φ(c). ■\blacksquare■

Read it as: near ccc, fff changes by "slope times displacement", where the slope φ(x)\varphi(x)φ(x) is allowed to wobble but settles to f′(c)f'(c)f′(c).

Chapter 2 — Rules of differentiation

Theorem (algebra of derivatives). Let f,gf, gf,g be differentiable at ccc and k∈Rk \in \mathbb{R}k∈R. Then

  • (f+g)′(c)=f′(c)+g′(c)(f + g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)(f+g)′(c)=f′(c)+g′(c) and (kf)′(c)=kf′(c)(kf)'(c) = k f'(c)(kf)′(c)=kf′(c);
  • (fg)′(c)=f′(c)g(c)+f(c)g′(c)(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)(fg)′(c)=f′(c)g(c)+f(c)g′(c);
  • if g(c)≠0g(c) \neq 0g(c)=0, then (f/g)′(c)=f′(c)g(c)−f(c)g′(c)g(c)2(f/g)'(c) = \dfrac{f'(c)g(c) - f(c)g'(c)}{g(c)^2}(f/g)′(c)=g(c)2f′(c)g(c)−f(c)g′(c)​.

Proof of the product rule. Add and subtract f(x)g(c)f(x)g(c)f(x)g(c):

f(x)g(x)−f(c)g(c)x−c=f(x) g(x)−g(c)x−c+g(c) f(x)−f(c)x−c.\frac{f(x)g(x) - f(c)g(c)}{x - c} = f(x)\,\frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c} + g(c)\,\frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c}. x−cf(x)g(x)−f(c)g(c)​=f(x)x−cg(x)−g(c)​+g(c)x−cf(x)−f(c)​.

As x→cx \to cx→c: f(x)→f(c)f(x) \to f(c)f(x)→f(c) because differentiable implies continuous, and the two quotients tend to g′(c)g'(c)g′(c) and f′(c)f'(c)f′(c). ■\blacksquare■

The sum rule is immediate from limit laws. For the quotient rule, first prove (1/g)′(c)=−g′(c)/g(c)2(1/g)'(c) = -g'(c)/g(c)^2(1/g)′(c)=−g′(c)/g(c)2 (note that g(x)≠0g(x) \neq 0g(x)=0 near ccc by continuity), then apply the product rule.

The chain rule, done properly

Theorem (chain rule). Let g:I→Rg : I \to \mathbb{R}g:I→R be differentiable at ccc, let g(I)⊆Jg(I) \subseteq Jg(I)⊆J for an interval JJJ, and let f:J→Rf : J \to \mathbb{R}f:J→R be differentiable at g(c)g(c)g(c). Then f∘gf \circ gf∘g is differentiable at ccc and

(f∘g)′(c)=f′(g(c))⋅g′(c).(f \circ g)'(c) = f'(g(c)) \cdot g'(c). (f∘g)′(c)=f′(g(c))⋅g′(c).

The tempting wrong proof. Write

f(g(x))−f(g(c))x−c=f(g(x))−f(g(c))g(x)−g(c)⋅g(x)−g(c)x−c\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{x - c} = \frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c} x−cf(g(x))−f(g(c))​=g(x)−g(c)f(g(x))−f(g(c))​⋅x−cg(x)−g(c)​

and let x→cx \to cx→c. This breaks whenever g(x)=g(c)g(x) = g(c)g(x)=g(c) for xxx arbitrarily close to ccc, because then you divide by zero infinitely often. That really happens: g(x)=x2sin⁡(1/x)g(x) = x^2 \sin(1/x)g(x)=x2sin(1/x) (with g(0)=0g(0) = 0g(0)=0) takes the value 000 at x=1/(nπ)x = 1/(n\pi)x=1/(nπ) for every integer n≥1n \geq 1n≥1.

Correct proof. By the lemma, there is ψ\psiψ continuous at d=g(c)d = g(c)d=g(c) with f(y)−f(d)=ψ(y)(y−d)f(y) - f(d) = \psi(y)(y - d)f(y)−f(d)=ψ(y)(y−d) for all y∈Jy \in Jy∈J, and ψ(d)=f′(d)\psi(d) = f'(d)ψ(d)=f′(d). There is also φ\varphiφ continuous at ccc with g(x)−g(c)=φ(x)(x−c)g(x) - g(c) = \varphi(x)(x - c)g(x)−g(c)=φ(x)(x−c) and φ(c)=g′(c)\varphi(c) = g'(c)φ(c)=g′(c). Put y=g(x)y = g(x)y=g(x):

f(g(x))−f(g(c))=ψ(g(x)) (g(x)−g(c))=ψ(g(x)) φ(x) (x−c).f(g(x)) - f(g(c)) = \psi(g(x))\,\bigl(g(x) - g(c)\bigr) = \psi(g(x))\,\varphi(x)\,(x - c). f(g(x))−f(g(c))=ψ(g(x))(g(x)−g(c))=ψ(g(x))φ(x)(x−c).

The function x↦ψ(g(x))φ(x)x \mapsto \psi(g(x))\varphi(x)x↦ψ(g(x))φ(x) is continuous at ccc: ggg is continuous at ccc, ψ\psiψ is continuous at g(c)g(c)g(c), and products of functions continuous at ccc are continuous at ccc. By the lemma again, f∘gf \circ gf∘g is differentiable at ccc with derivative ψ(g(c))φ(c)=f′(g(c)) g′(c)\psi(g(c))\varphi(c) = f'(g(c))\,g'(c)ψ(g(c))φ(c)=f′(g(c))g′(c). ■\blacksquare■

No division by g(x)−g(c)g(x) - g(c)g(x)−g(c) appears anywhere.

Trick: whenever a proof wants to divide by something that might be zero, try the Carathéodory form. It turns "limit of a quotient" into "continuity of a factor", and continuity composes cleanly.

Chapter 3 — Extrema, Rolle and the Mean Value Theorem

Interior extremum theorem

Theorem. Let f:(a,b)→Rf : (a, b) \to \mathbb{R}f:(a,b)→R have a maximum (or minimum) at c∈(a,b)c \in (a, b)c∈(a,b), and let fff be differentiable at ccc. Then f′(c)=0f'(c) = 0f′(c)=0.

Proof (maximum case). For x>cx > cx>c we have f(x)−f(c)≤0f(x) - f(c) \leq 0f(x)−f(c)≤0 and x−c>0x - c > 0x−c>0, so the difference quotient is ≤0\leq 0≤0; the right-hand limit gives f′(c)≤0f'(c) \leq 0f′(c)≤0. For x<cx < cx<c the numerator is ≤0\leq 0≤0 and the denominator <0< 0<0, so the quotient is ≥0\geq 0≥0; the left-hand limit gives f′(c)≥0f'(c) \geq 0f′(c)≥0. Hence f′(c)=0f'(c) = 0f′(c)=0. ■\blacksquare■

Watch out: the point must be interior. f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x on [0,1][0, 1][0,1] has its maximum at 111 and f′(1)=1f'(1) = 1f′(1)=1. And the converse fails: f(x)=x3f(x) = x^3f(x)=x3 has f′(0)=0f'(0) = 0f′(0)=0 but no extremum at 000.

Rolle's theorem

Theorem (Rolle). Let fff be continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b] and differentiable on (a,b)(a, b)(a,b), with f(a)=f(b)f(a) = f(b)f(a)=f(b). Then there is c∈(a,b)c \in (a, b)c∈(a,b) with f′(c)=0f'(c) = 0f′(c)=0.

Proof. By the Extreme Value Theorem (post 02), fff attains a maximum MMM and a minimum mmm on the compact set [a,b][a, b][a,b]. If both are attained only at the endpoints, then M=m=f(a)M = m = f(a)M=m=f(a) and fff is constant, so f′(c)=0f'(c) = 0f′(c)=0 for every c∈(a,b)c \in (a, b)c∈(a,b). Otherwise one of them is attained at some interior ccc, and the interior extremum theorem gives f′(c)=0f'(c) = 0f′(c)=0. ■\blacksquare■

All three hypotheses matter. Continuity at the endpoints: f(x)=xf(x) = xf(x)=x on [0,1)[0,1)[0,1) with f(1)=0f(1) = 0f(1)=0. Differentiability inside: ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣ on [−1,1][-1, 1][−1,1]. Equal end values: xxx on [0,1][0, 1][0,1].

The Mean Value Theorem

Theorem (MVT). Let fff be continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b] and differentiable on (a,b)(a, b)(a,b). Then there is c∈(a,b)c \in (a, b)c∈(a,b) with

f′(c)=f(b)−f(a)b−a.f'(c) = \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}. f′(c)=b−af(b)−f(a)​.

Geometrically: somewhere the tangent line is parallel to the secant line through the end points.

Proof. Subtract the secant line. Let

h(x)=f(x)−(f(a)+f(b)−f(a)b−a (x−a)).h(x) = f(x) - \left( f(a) + \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}\,(x - a) \right). h(x)=f(x)−(f(a)+b−af(b)−f(a)​(x−a)).

Then hhh is continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b], differentiable on (a,b)(a, b)(a,b), and h(a)=h(b)=0h(a) = h(b) = 0h(a)=h(b)=0. Rolle gives c∈(a,b)c \in (a, b)c∈(a,b) with 0=h′(c)=f′(c)−f(b)−f(a)b−a0 = h'(c) = f'(c) - \frac{f(b) - f(a)}{b - a}0=h′(c)=f′(c)−b−af(b)−f(a)​. ■\blacksquare■

Worked example. f(x)=x3f(x) = x^3f(x)=x3 on [0,2][0, 2][0,2]. The secant slope is 8−02−0=4\frac{8 - 0}{2 - 0} = 42−08−0​=4. Solve f′(c)=3c2=4f'(c) = 3c^2 = 4f′(c)=3c2=4 in (0,2)(0, 2)(0,2): c=23≈1.1547c = \frac{2}{\sqrt 3} \approx 1.1547c=3​2​≈1.1547. The theorem only promises that such a ccc exists; here you can find it.

Consequences

Corollary 1 (zero derivative). If f′(x)=0f'(x) = 0f′(x)=0 for every xxx in an interval III, then fff is constant on III.

Proof. Take x<yx < yx<y in III. The MVT on [x,y][x, y][x,y] gives f(y)−f(x)=f′(c)(y−x)=0f(y) - f(x) = f'(c)(y - x) = 0f(y)−f(x)=f′(c)(y−x)=0. ■\blacksquare■

The interval matters: f(x)=sign⁡(x)f(x) = \operatorname{sign}(x)f(x)=sign(x) on R∖{0}\mathbb{R} \setminus \{0\}R∖{0} has f′=0f' = 0f′=0 everywhere on its domain but is not constant, because the domain is not an interval.

Corollary 2 (same derivative). If f′=g′f' = g'f′=g′ on an interval, then f−gf - gf−g is constant. This is why antiderivatives are unique "up to +C+C+C".

Corollary 3 (monotonicity). On an interval III, with fff differentiable on III:

Hypothesis on the interval Conclusion
f′≥0f' \geq 0f′≥0 fff is increasing (x<y⇒f(x)≤f(y)x < y \Rightarrow f(x) \leq f(y)x<y⇒f(x)≤f(y))
f′>0f' > 0f′>0 fff is strictly increasing
f′≤0f' \leq 0f′≤0 or f′<0f' < 0f′<0 decreasing or strictly decreasing
∣f′∣≤M\lvert f'\rvert \leq M∣f′∣≤M ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤M∣x−y∣\lvert f(x) - f(y)\rvert \leq M\lvert x - y\rvert∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤M∣x−y∣ (Lipschitz)

Each line is one application of f(y)−f(x)=f′(c)(y−x)f(y) - f(x) = f'(c)(y - x)f(y)−f(x)=f′(c)(y−x). The converse of line 2 fails: x3x^3x3 is strictly increasing but f′(0)=0f'(0) = 0f′(0)=0.

Worked example: a Lipschitz bound. Since ∣cos⁡∣≤1\lvert \cos\rvert \leq 1∣cos∣≤1, the last line gives ∣sin⁡a−sin⁡b∣≤∣a−b∣\lvert \sin a - \sin b\rvert \leq \lvert a - b\rvert∣sina−sinb∣≤∣a−b∣ for all real a,ba, ba,b.

Worked example: estimating a square root. Apply the MVT to x\sqrt{x}x​ on [100,101][100, 101][100,101]: 101−10=12c\sqrt{101} - 10 = \frac{1}{2\sqrt c}101​−10=2c​1​ for some c∈(100,101)c \in (100, 101)c∈(100,101). Since 10<c<10110 < \sqrt c < \sqrt{101}10<c​<101​,

0.04975…=12101<101−10<120=0.05.0.04975\ldots = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{101}} < \sqrt{101} - 10 < \frac{1}{20} = 0.05. 0.04975…=2101​1​<101​−10<201​=0.05.

The true value is 101−10=0.049875…\sqrt{101} - 10 = 0.049875\ldots101​−10=0.049875…, inside the bracket.

Cauchy's generalised Mean Value Theorem

Theorem (Cauchy MVT). Let f,gf, gf,g be continuous on [a,b][a, b][a,b] and differentiable on (a,b)(a, b)(a,b). Then there is c∈(a,b)c \in (a, b)c∈(a,b) with

(f(b)−f(a)) g′(c)=(g(b)−g(a)) f′(c).\bigl(f(b) - f(a)\bigr)\,g'(c) = \bigl(g(b) - g(a)\bigr)\,f'(c). (f(b)−f(a))g′(c)=(g(b)−g(a))f′(c).

Proof. Let h(x)=(f(b)−f(a))g(x)−(g(b)−g(a))f(x)h(x) = \bigl(f(b) - f(a)\bigr) g(x) - \bigl(g(b) - g(a)\bigr) f(x)h(x)=(f(b)−f(a))g(x)−(g(b)−g(a))f(x). A direct computation gives h(a)=f(b)g(a)−g(b)f(a)=h(b)h(a) = f(b)g(a) - g(b)f(a) = h(b)h(a)=f(b)g(a)−g(b)f(a)=h(b). Rolle gives ccc with h′(c)=0h'(c) = 0h′(c)=0, which is the claim. ■\blacksquare■

With g(x)=xg(x) = xg(x)=x this is the ordinary MVT. The version with two functions is what L'Hôpital's rule needs.

Chapter 4 — Derivatives are not arbitrary functions

A derivative that is not continuous

Let

g(x)={x2sin⁡(1/x)x≠0,0x=0.g(x) = \begin{cases} x^2 \sin(1/x) & x \neq 0, \\ 0 & x = 0. \end{cases} g(x)={x2sin(1/x)0​x=0,x=0.​

At 000: ∣g(x)−g(0)x∣=∣xsin⁡(1/x)∣≤∣x∣→0\left\lvert \frac{g(x) - g(0)}{x} \right\rvert = \lvert x \sin(1/x)\rvert \leq \lvert x\rvert \to 0​xg(x)−g(0)​​=∣xsin(1/x)∣≤∣x∣→0, so g′(0)=0g'(0) = 0g′(0)=0. For x≠0x \neq 0x=0 the ordinary rules give

g′(x)=2xsin⁡(1/x)−cos⁡(1/x).g'(x) = 2x\sin(1/x) - \cos(1/x). g′(x)=2xsin(1/x)−cos(1/x).

As x→0x \to 0x→0 the first term tends to 000 but cos⁡(1/x)\cos(1/x)cos(1/x) oscillates between −1-1−1 and 111 for ever. So g′g'g′ exists at every point of R\mathbb{R}R, yet lim⁡x→0g′(x)\lim_{x \to 0} g'(x)limx→0​g′(x) does not exist. A function can be differentiable everywhere with a discontinuous derivative. In the notation of Chapter 1: ggg is differentiable on R\mathbb{R}R but g∉C1(R)g \notin C^1(\mathbb{R})g∈/C1(R).

Darboux's theorem

Discontinuous derivatives still cannot jump. They always have the intermediate value property.

Theorem (Darboux). Let fff be differentiable on [a,b][a, b][a,b] (one-sided at the endpoints). If yyy lies strictly between f′(a)f'(a)f′(a) and f′(b)f'(b)f′(b), then there is c∈(a,b)c \in (a, b)c∈(a,b) with f′(c)=yf'(c) = yf′(c)=y.

Then ggg is differentiable on [a,b][a, b][a,b] with g′(a)=f′(a)−y<0g'(a) = f'(a) - y < 0g′(a)=f′(a)−y<0 and g′(b)=f′(b)−y>0g'(b) = f'(b) - y > 0g′(b)=f′(b)−y>0.   • c≠ac \neq ac=a: since g′(a)<0g'(a) < 0g′(a)<0, the quotient g(x)−g(a)x−a\frac{g(x) - g(a)}{x - a}x−ag(x)−g(a)​ is negative for xxx slightly bigger than aaa, so g(x)<g(a)g(x) < g(a)g(x)<g(a) there, and aaa is not a minimum.

So c∈(a,b)c \in (a, b)c∈(a,b) and the interior extremum theorem gives g′(c)=0g'(c) = 0g′(c)=0, that is, f′(c)=yf'(c) = yf′(c)=y. ■\blacksquare■

Chapter 7 — Smooth, analytic, and the monsters

Smooth but not analytic

Let

f(x)={e−1/x2x≠0,0x=0.f(x) = \begin{cases} e^{-1/x^2} & x \neq 0, \\ 0 & x = 0. \end{cases} f(x)={e−1/x20​x=0,x=0.​

Claim. fff is C∞C^\inftyC∞ on R\mathbb{R}R and f(k)(0)=0f^{(k)}(0) = 0f(k)(0)=0 for every k≥0k \geq 0k≥0.

Sketch of proof. For x≠0x \neq 0x=0, induction shows f(k)(x)=pk(1/x) e−1/x2f^{(k)}(x) = p_k(1/x)\,e^{-1/x^2}f(k)(x)=pk​(1/x)e−1/x2 for some polynomial pkp_kpk​. At 000, use the definition and induction: f(k)(x)−0x=1xpk(1/x)e−1/x2\frac{f^{(k)}(x) - 0}{x} = \frac1x p_k(1/x) e^{-1/x^2}xf(k)(x)−0​=x1​pk​(1/x)e−1/x2, and with t=1/xt = 1/xt=1/x this is a polynomial in ttt times e−t2e^{-t^2}e−t2, which tends to 000 as ∣t∣→∞\lvert t\rvert \to \infty∣t∣→∞ because et2e^{t^2}et2 outgrows every power of ttt. So f(k+1)(0)=0f^{(k+1)}(0) = 0f(k+1)(0)=0. ■\blacksquare■

Consequently every Taylor polynomial of fff at 000 is the zero polynomial, and Rn(x)=f(x)>0R_n(x) = f(x) > 0Rn​(x)=f(x)>0 for every x≠0x \neq 0x=0 and every nnn. The Taylor series at 000 converges everywhere, to the wrong function. So "infinitely differentiable" does not imply "equal to its Taylor series". A function that equals its Taylor series near each point is called (real) analytic; this fff is smooth but not analytic at 000. Taylor's theorem is not wrong here: it only claims the remainder has the Lagrange form, and here the remainder simply does not go to 000. Post 05 returns to this with power series.

Continuous but nowhere differentiable

Theorem (Weierstrass, 1872). Let 0<a<10 < a < 10<a<1, let bbb be an odd positive integer, and let ab>1+3π2ab > 1 + \frac{3\pi}{2}ab>1+23π​. Then

W(x)=∑n=0∞ancos⁡(bnπx)W(x) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a^n \cos(b^n \pi x) W(x)=n=0∑∞​ancos(bnπx)

is continuous at every x∈Rx \in \mathbb{R}x∈R and differentiable at no x∈Rx \in \mathbb{R}x∈R.

For example, a=12a = \frac12a=21​, b=13b = 13b=13 gives ab=6.5>1+3π2≈5.712ab = 6.5 > 1 + \frac{3\pi}{2} \approx 5.712ab=6.5>1+23π​≈5.712. Continuity comes from the Weierstrass M-test of post 05: ∣ancos⁡(bnπx)∣≤an\lvert a^n \cos(b^n \pi x)\rvert \leq a^n∣ancos(bnπx)∣≤an and ∑an\sum a^n∑an converges, so the series converges uniformly, and uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous. The non-differentiability proof is a careful estimate of difference quotients (Hardy showed in 1916 that ab≥1ab \geq 1ab≥1 is enough). The picture to keep: the graph has corners at every scale, like ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣ at 000, but everywhere.

The hierarchy

Class Example that is in this class but not the next
continuous ∣x∣\lvert x\rvert∣x∣ (not differentiable at 0)
differentiable x2sin⁡(1/x)x^2\sin(1/x)x2sin(1/x) (derivative not continuous at 0)

Each row is strictly larger than the next. Weierstrass's WWW sits in row 1 and is as far from row 2 as possible.

Exercise 6. Suppose f:R→Rf : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}f:R→R satisfies ∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤(x−y)2\lvert f(x) - f(y)\rvert \leq (x - y)^2∣f(x)−f(y)∣≤(x−y)2 for all x,yx, yx,y. Prove that fff is constant.

Solution

For x≠yx \neq yx=y, ∣f(x)−f(y)x−y∣≤∣x−y∣\left\lvert \frac{f(x) - f(y)}{x - y}\right\rvert \leq \lvert x - y\rvert​x−yf(x)−f(y)​​≤∣x−y∣. Letting x→yx \to yx→y gives f′(y)=0f'(y) = 0f′(y)=0 for every yyy. By Corollary 1 of the MVT on the interval R\mathbb{R}R, fff is constant.

Exercise 7. Can the floor function ⌊x⌋\lfloor x \rfloor⌊x⌋ be the derivative of some function FFF on [0,2][0, 2][0,2]?

Solution

No. On [0,2][0, 2][0,2] the floor function takes the values 000, 111 and 222 but never 12\frac1221​. If F′=⌊x⌋F' = \lfloor x \rfloorF′=⌊x⌋ on [0,2][0, 2][0,2], Darboux's theorem on [0,1][0, 1][0,1] (where F′(0)=0F'(0) = 0F′(0)=0 and F′(1)=1F'(1) = 1F′(1)=1) would give ccc with F′(c)=12F'(c) = \frac12F′(c)=21​. Contradiction.

What's next

Post 04 builds the Riemann integral from scratch: partitions, upper and lower Darboux sums, the Riemann criterion, and proofs that continuous and monotone functions are integrable. The Mean Value Theorem from this post is the engine of the proof of the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus there, and a relative of x2sin⁡(1/x)x^2\sin(1/x)x2sin(1/x) returns as a warning about what that theorem needs.

References

  • Stephen Abbott, Understanding Analysis, 2nd ed., Springer (Undergraduate Texts in Mathematics), 2015 — Chapter 5, "The Derivative", including Darboux's theorem and a continuous nowhere-differentiable function.
  • Walter Rudin, Principles of Mathematical Analysis, 3rd ed., McGraw-Hill, 1976 — Chapter 5 (Theorems 5.10 MVT, 5.12 Darboux, 5.13 L'Hôpital, 5.15 Taylor).
  • Robert G. Bartle and Donald R. Sherbert, Introduction to Real Analysis, 4th ed., Wiley, 2011 — Chapter 6, including the Carathéodory form of the chain rule.
  • Michael Spivak, Calculus, 4th ed., Publish or Perish, 2008 — Chapters 10–11 and 20 (Taylor polynomials and remainders).
  • Jiří Lebl, Basic Analysis I: Introduction to Real Analysis, free textbook — jirka.org/ra, Chapter 4.
  • MIT OpenCourseWare, 18.100A Real Analysis (Fall 2020), lecture notes on differentiation and Taylor's theorem.
  • G. H. Hardy, "Weierstrass's non-differentiable function", Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 17 (1916), 301–325.

Note: this post is in progress. Planned additions: the Peano and integral forms of the Taylor remainder, convex functions and the second-derivative test, a full proof that the Weierstrass function is nowhere differentiable, and Newton's method with its quadratic error bound.
